analysis.one_liner: Treats US-owned corporations set up in tax-haven countries as domestic companies for tax purposes.
analysis.headline: A bill to make US-owned companies in tax havens pay US taxes was sent to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2005 and never got a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: US companies can set up subsidiaries in low-tax countries like the Cayman Islands or Bermuda and park profits there to avoid US taxes. This bill would treat those subsidiaries as American companies for tax purposes, so their profits would be taxed by the United States. It listed dozens of tax-haven countries, let the Treasury add or remove countries from the list, and exempted subsidiaries doing real business in the country where they were created. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: US taxpayers generally. Profits shifted offshore to tax havens currently go untaxed by the United States; taxing them would bring in revenue that could reduce taxes on others or fund public programs, and would level the playing field for companies that don't use offshore shelters.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would treat a foreign corporation controlled by US owners as a domestic corporation if it was created in any of dozens of listed tax-haven countries, subjecting its income to US tax.
The bill let the Treasury Secretary add or remove countries from the tax-haven list, so companies could not simply move to a new haven to escape it.
It exempted subsidiaries whose income comes almost entirely from genuinely doing business in the country where they were created, targeting paper companies rather than real foreign operations.

analysis.who_pays: US multinational corporations that use subsidiaries in tax-haven countries to keep profits out of US taxation; they would owe more US tax.

drawbacks.text: Treating tax-haven subsidiaries as domestic could discourage US companies from having legitimate operations in those small economies, despite the exception for real local business activity.
A unilateral US rule could put American multinational firms at a disadvantage against foreign competitors that face no comparable tax on profits booked in low-tax jurisdictions.

Defining tax havens by a fixed country list is blunt: companies and jurisdictions change behavior, and even with Treasury flexibility the line between a haven and a legitimate low-tax business location is contested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real and large tax-avoidance channel: US-owned paper companies in tax havens that exist mainly to defer or escape US tax. The main costs fall on the corporations doing this, though the blunt country-list approach and competitive concerns are fair objections. The exception for companies doing real business locally addresses the biggest worry about punishing genuine foreign operations.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee when introduced and sat there for the rest of the Congress; the committee never acted on it and it never reached the floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Byron Dorgan introduced the bill on April 13, 2005, joined by Sen. Carl Levin, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
The Finance Committee held no hearings, marked it up, or scheduled no further action; the bill's only recorded actions after referral are Dorgan's introductory remarks on February 1, 2006.
The bill never came to a vote in the Senate or the House before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US multinational corporations using tax-haven subsidiaries kept the ability to shift profits offshore untaxed, since the bill died in committee without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies sheltering profits in tax havens

for.name: Sen. Byron Dorgan
for.role: Senator from North Dakota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks for it in 2005 and again in February 2006.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in April 2005 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and both cosponsors were Democrats, and the tax-writing Finance Committee, chaired by a Republican, never acted on the bill; no votes were ever taken, so no bipartisan support was tested.

industries.industry: US multinational corporations using tax-haven subsidiaries
industries.note: The bill would end their ability to book profits in places like Bermuda and the Cayman Islands to escape US tax. They benefit from the current rules the bill would change, at the cost of federal revenue that other taxpayers ultimately cover.
Places like the Cayman Islands and Bermuda profit from hosting US-owned paper companies. Treating those companies as domestic would reduce the demand for their incorporation services.
